meta_how_title: How oko works — camera, bridge, cloud
meta_how_desc: A small bridge program on any mini-PC finds your cameras, pushes the stream out to the cloud and keeps a rolling archive. Nothing is exposed to the internet.

hero_title: Your cameras keep recording. Even when the recorder is gone.
hero_sub: oko connects the cameras you already own to a cloud archive. The footage lives off-site, so losing the building does not mean losing the evidence.
hero_note: Works with Hikvision, Dahua, Reolink, Uniview and any other RTSP or ONVIF camera.
brands_label: Works out of the box with
brands_any: …and any other camera that speaks RTSP or ONVIF
retention_title: Seven days of archive. Free, for every camera.
retention_body: The cloud keeps a rolling seven days of continuous recording at no charge — not a trial, not a teaser. Older footage deletes itself as new footage arrives. Elsewhere this exact thing is the paid plan.
pricing_sub: Free covers a home. When paid tiers launch, they will stay cheaper than anything comparable — the prices below are the ones we commit to.
plan_f_browser: Live and archive in the browser
pricing_note: Everything is free today, while we work with the first customers. The tiers above take effect when billing launches — connecting now keeps you on Free.
pricing_compare: For reference: 7-day cloud recording runs $3–6 per camera monthly elsewhere.
value_1_body: A recorder in the building can be stolen, burned or simply taken. Footage that already left the site cannot be taken with it — that is the whole point of recording elsewhere.
value_2_title: Nothing is exposed to the internet
value_2_body: No port forwarding, no static IP, no camera hanging open on a public address. The bridge opens the connection outward, so there is nothing to scan and nothing to reach from the outside.
value_3_body: No replacing hardware and no vendor lock. If a camera speaks RTSP or ONVIF — and installer-grade cameras do — it works.
step_1_body: One command on any Linux box already in the camera network — a mini-PC, a Raspberry Pi, an old office machine. No Docker required.
step_2_body: The bridge scans the local network over ONVIF and reports what it found. You enter the camera password, nothing else.
step_3_body: Live view and the archive open in a browser. Scrub the timeline, save a clip, close the tab.
how_intro: Between your camera and your browser there is exactly one moving part you install yourself. Everything else is ours to run.
how_bridge_body: A small program on a machine inside your camera network. It pulls the stream from the camera over the local network and pushes it out to the cloud over an encrypted connection it opens itself. Because the connection goes outward, your network needs no incoming rules, no static IP and no changes on the router.
how_bridge_req: It runs on anything with Linux and a network port: a €60 mini-PC, a Raspberry Pi 4, a spare laptop. One bridge serves every camera on that network.
how_cloud_body: Incoming streams are recorded continuously and kept for seven days on a rolling basis — the oldest footage is deleted automatically as new footage arrives. Live view uses WebRTC for low latency; the archive plays back over HLS.
how_access_body: Cameras belong to your account and only your account. Every request for a stream is authorised individually — there are no public links and no broadcast pages. That is a deliberate choice, not a setting we forgot.
how_offline_body: The bridge reconnects on its own and resumes pushing. Anything the camera recorded to its own SD card during the outage stays on the camera — the cloud archive shows the gap honestly rather than pretending it saw something.
faq_a1: Anything that speaks RTSP or ONVIF, which covers essentially all installer-grade hardware: Hikvision, Dahua, Reolink, Uniview and their many rebrands. Tapo and Imou cameras can work too, with the caveat that their firmware sometimes hides the RTSP switch behind a cloud account. Cheap P2P-only cameras — the ones that only ever work through the vendor's own app — are not supported yet.
faq_a2: Seven days, rolling. Older footage is deleted automatically as new footage comes in. Longer retention is on the roadmap, not in the product today.
faq_q3: Do I need a static IP or port forwarding?
faq_a3: No. The bridge opens the connection outward, the same way your browser does. Nothing needs to be reachable from the internet, which also means there is nothing for a scanner to find.
faq_q4: What hardware does the bridge need?
faq_a4: Very little. Any Linux machine on the same network as the cameras: a mini-PC, a Raspberry Pi 4, an old office desktop. It mostly orchestrates ffmpeg, so it does not need to be fast — it needs to stay powered on.
faq_a5: You. Streams and archives are tied to your account and every playback request is authorised individually. There are no public links. Support access to a customer account requires your explicit consent, is time-limited and is written to an audit log.
faq_q6: What happens if the camera or the recorder is destroyed?
faq_a6: Everything already uploaded stays in the cloud and remains available from your account. That is the reason to record off-site in the first place.
faq_a7: One bridge covers every camera on its network. Practically the ceiling is the upload bandwidth of that site, not the software.
faq_a8: The Free tier is permanent: seven days of rolling archive for up to two cameras, full resolution. Paid tiers are coming — Start at $2.49 per camera per month keeps the same 7 days with no camera limit, Plus at $4.99 keeps 30 days. Until billing launches, everything is free.
